intro: You already understand casual English at full speed: gonna, dunno, kinda, and film slang like I'm down and gutted. Now it's time to use it yourself, with good judgment: the informal words that make you sound relaxed (reckon, fancy, no worries), the slang that's safe and the slang that isn't, and the British and American words that differ (in London, never compliment someone's pants!). Warm-up: which bahasa gaul words do you use with friends but never in a meeting?
teachingNotes: Recap and build, one line each, don't re-teach: c2-listening-native-speed taught the learner to UNDERSTAND reduced forms (gonna, wanna, gotta, kinda, sorta, dunno, lemme, gimme), fillers, vague language (and stuff, or whatever, -ish) and film slang by country (US I'm down, my bad, bail, I'm beat; UK gutted, knackered, chuffed, cheers; UK/AU mate); c2-idiomatic-mastery taught 'recognise everything, produce the safe ones' and register for idioms; c1-register the formal / neutral / informal scale and mixed-register messages ('Hey Mr Tan, wanna catch up?'); c1-world-englishes lift/elevator, flat/apartment, holiday/vacation, ground floor/first floor and Australian No worries; b2-formal-informal-vocab 'Hi Sir, I wanna ask about the job'. New at C2: PRODUCING informal English correctly and appropriately, judging slang safety, and a fuller everyday UK/US word set with its traps.

Informal spoken English (objective informal-spoken). gonna = going to + a verb, so the be stays: I'm / you're / she's / we're / they're gonna; never + a place (I'm going to Bandung, not 'I'm gonna Bandung'). wanna = want to: I / you / they wanna, but she wants to (not 'she wanna'). gotta = have got to: 'I gotta go' is normal speech because it comes from I've got to (the 've disappears), which is why it seems to break the rule. Be honest that in fast QUESTIONS natives drop the first word ('You coming?', 'You gonna eat that?'), but statements keep the be. Hedges / vague words for use: kind of, sort of (agak, semacam), -ish (sevenish = sekitar jam tujuh; 'Ish.' alone = sort of), a bit (agak; British understatement: a bit annoyed can mean quite angry), or something, and stuff / and things. Everyday informal words: reckon (think; British/Australian, can sound rural in the US), fancy (British: want; 'Fancy a coffee?'; with a person = be attracted to: 'I fancy him' = naksir; Indonesians know fancy only as 'mewah'), cheers (British: thanks / bye / a toast), mate (UK/AU friend; address, mostly between men), guys ('Hi guys', 'you guys' = everyone, women included, casual US/UK; in written work messages Hi all / Hi everyone is safer), no worries (no problem / you're welcome), my bad (US, casual, small mistakes only), to be fair (British: adds a point on the other side), you know what I mean? (checks the listener; tiring if overused). The node's common errors: 'I gonna call you later' (Indonesian has no to be: 'aku mau telepon') → I'm gonna (speech) / I'm going to; 'Dear Sir or Madam, I wanna ask about the job' → 'Dear Sir or Madam, I would like to ask about the job' (spoken forms never go in emails, least of all with the most formal opening).

Slang with care (objective slang-with-care). Bridge: bahasa gaul (mager = malas gerak, gabut, anjay): fine with friends, never 'Maaf, Pak, saya mager' to a director; some gaul words date, some are rude to some people. English is the same. Common, fairly safe slang for casual talk (not formal writing): cool (That's cool = it's fine), awesome, chill / chill out, broke (bokek), a rip-off (far too expensive; rip someone off), a buck (US $1, ten bucks) / a quid (UK £1, ten quid, never 'quids'), FOMO. Younger / internet slang (understand; use only with people who use it): sus (suspicious), lowkey (a little, secretly), highkey (openly, very), vibe (atmosphere), ghost someone (stop replying with no explanation). Slang dates fast (groovy sounds 1970s; sick = great to young speakers, ill to everyone else) and belongs to groups; from an older manager, youth slang can sound try-hard; never overuse it at work. Three questions: who, where (channel), would they use it themselves? Neutral swaps: broke → short of money, a rip-off → overpriced, awesome → excellent. OFFENSIVE WORDS ARE NOT TAUGHT: if the learner asks, say some slang is offensive (swear words, insults about groups), that hearing it in films doesn't make it safe, and 'when in doubt, leave it out'. Don't list or explain specific offensive words.

UK / US vocabulary (objective uk-us-vocabulary): flat/apartment, lift/elevator, holiday/vacation (US holiday = a public holiday), queue/line (stand in line), rubbish/trash or garbage (UK rubbish also = nonsense), biscuit/cookie (US biscuit = soft savoury bread roll), pavement/sidewalk (US pavement = road surface), mobile/cell phone, petrol/gas (gasoline), trousers/pants, football/soccer (US football = American football), CV/résumé (US CV = long academic one), autumn/fall, the bill/the check (restaurant; UK cheque = US check from a bank), ground floor/first floor (UK first floor = US second floor = lantai 2 in buildings where the street level is lantai 1; many Indonesian malls with a Lantai Dasar / G count like the UK, so test the UK↔US equivalence, not a lantai number). Bridge: Indonesians already say lift and CV (British), and HP / handphone, which neither country uses (mobile / cell phone). Advice: understand both, pick one for your own writing and be consistent; either is correct. The node's common error: 'I like your pants' meaning trousers, in the UK → 'I like your trousers' (British pants = underwear). Accept résumé / resume and cell phone / cellphone / cell.

Testing and limits: at C2 all grammar is available; this is a vocabulary and judgment lesson, and much of register is style, so only test clear cases (a missing be before gonna, chat vs a formal email to a stranger, youth slang in a post the regional director reads, a UK/US word when the country is named). Answers are short: accept any wording with the right meaning for slang meanings. Audio is one plain TTS voice: nothing depends on accent or tone, and no listen item depends on how a word sounds. Don't add more slang unless asked; if asked, give the meaning, an Indonesian gloss, the register and who uses it. All dialogues are original practice texts.

keyPoints.title: Informal speech: relaxed, but still grammatical
keyPoints.explanation: gonna replaces going to, so the be stays: I'm gonna, she's gonna, we're gonna (never 'I gonna'). wanna = want to (she wants to, not 'she wanna'); I gotta go is fine because it comes from I've got to. Hedges and vague words (kind of, sort of, -ish, a bit, or something, and stuff) make you sound relaxed. Everyday informal words: reckon (think), fancy (want, British), cheers (thanks / bye, British), mate, guys, no worries, my bad, to be fair, you know what I mean? All of these are for conversation and chats; a formal email needs formal words (Dear Sir or Madam, I am writing to ask …).

examples.en: I'm gonna call you after the meeting, OK?
examples.id: Aku telepon kamu habis rapat, ya?

examples.en: I reckon the client will say yes.

id.title: Bahasa lisan informal: santai, tapi tetap benar
id.explanation: gonna menggantikan going to, jadi be-nya tetap ada: I'm gonna, she's gonna, we're gonna (tidak pernah 'I gonna'). wanna = want to (she wants to, bukan 'she wanna'); I gotta go itu wajar karena berasal dari I've got to. Pelunak dan kata-kata samar (kind of, sort of, -ish, a bit, or something, and stuff) membuatmu terdengar santai. Kosakata santai sehari-hari: reckon (rasa, kira), fancy (mau, Inggris), cheers (makasih / dah, Inggris), mate, guys, no worries, my bad, to be fair, you know what I mean? Semua ini untuk obrolan dan chat; email formal butuh kata-kata formal (Dear Sir or Madam, I am writing to ask …).

keyPoints.title: Slang: understand lots, use a little
keyPoints.explanation: Common, fairly safe slang for casual talk: cool, awesome, chill, broke (no money), a rip-off (far too expensive), a buck (US $1) / a quid (UK £1), FOMO. Younger and internet slang: sus (suspicious), lowkey / highkey, vibe, ghost someone (disappear without a word). Slang dates fast and belongs to groups (age, region, online communities), so keep it out of work emails, reports and posts to people you don't know well, and don't overuse youth slang at work. Some slang is offensive: when in doubt, leave it out. It's like bahasa gaul: mager and gabut with friends, not with your director.

examples.en: I can't come to Bali this month: I'm broke.
examples.id: Aku nggak bisa ikut ke Bali bulan ini: lagi bokek.

examples.en: The new café in Kemang has a really nice vibe.
examples.id: Kafe baru di Kemang suasananya enak banget.

examples.en: Work email: The quotation seems rather high. Could you review it?
examples.id: Email kerja: Penawaran harganya tampak cukup tinggi. Bisakah Anda meninjaunya kembali?

id.title: Slang: pahami banyak, pakai sedikit
id.explanation: Slang yang umum dan cukup aman untuk obrolan santai: cool, awesome, chill, broke (bokek), a rip-off (kemahalan), a buck (1 dolar AS) / a quid (1 pound Inggris), FOMO. Slang anak muda dan internet: sus (mencurigakan), lowkey / highkey, vibe, ghost someone (menghilang tanpa kabar). Slang cepat ketinggalan zaman dan milik kelompok tertentu (usia, daerah, komunitas online), jadi jangan pakai di email kerja, laporan, dan unggahan untuk orang yang belum kamu kenal baik, dan jangan berlebihan memakai slang anak muda di kantor. Sebagian slang itu kasar: kalau ragu, jangan dipakai. Sama seperti bahasa gaul: mager dan gabut dengan teman, bukan dengan direktur.

keyPoints.title: British and American words
keyPoints.explanation: UK / US: flat / apartment, lift / elevator, holiday / vacation, queue / line, rubbish / trash, biscuit / cookie, pavement / sidewalk, mobile / cell phone, petrol / gas, trousers / pants, football / soccer, CV / résumé, autumn / fall, the bill / the check (in a restaurant). Traps: British pants = underwear; the British first floor is one level above the street (the street level is the ground floor), while the American first floor is the street level, so British first floor = American second floor. Understand both; choose one for your own writing and be consistent.

examples.en: UK: Our flat is next to the lift. · US: Our apartment is next to the elevator.
UK: We're going on holiday in autumn. · US: We're going on vacation in the fall.
examples.id: Kami akan liburan di musim gugur.

examples.en: UK: Can I try on these trousers? (In the UK, pants = underwear.)
examples.id: Boleh saya coba celana panjang ini? (Di Inggris, pants = celana dalam.)

id.title: Kosakata Inggris dan Amerika
id.explanation: UK / US: flat / apartment, lift / elevator, holiday / vacation, queue / line, rubbish / trash, biscuit / cookie, pavement / sidewalk, mobile / cell phone, petrol / gas, trousers / pants, football / soccer, CV / résumé, autumn / fall, the bill / the check (di restoran). Jebakan: pants versi Inggris = celana dalam; first floor versi Inggris adalah satu lantai di atas level jalan (level jalan disebut ground floor), sedangkan first floor versi Amerika adalah lantai di level jalan, jadi first floor versi Inggris = second floor versi Amerika. Pahami keduanya; pilih salah satu untuk tulisanmu sendiri dan konsistenlah.

guidedPractice.prompt: Correct this casual sentence: 'My sister wanna join us at the warung.'
expected: my sister wants to join us at the warung
my sister wants to join us
guidedPractice.hint: wanna = want to, and it only works where 'want' has no -s: I wanna, you wanna, but she ___ to.

guidedPractice.prompt: Tom (British) says: 'I reckon the rain will stop by four.' Write one neutral verb that can replace 'reckon'.
guidedPractice.hint: kayaknya / menurutku: what you do when you give an opinion.

guidedPractice.prompt: Write one casual word that means 'around eight o'clock', as in 'Let's meet at ___.'
Dimas: 'Sorry, I can't come to the concert. I'm totally broke till payday.' What does 'broke' mean here? Answer in a few English words.
Change to American English: 'There was a long queue at the post office.' Write the American word for 'queue'.

independentPractice.prompt: Your friend says: 'That new coffee shop in Blok M has a really nice vibe.' Write one neutral word with the same meaning as 'vibe' here.
An American friend asks: 'Can you take out the trash before you leave?' Write the British word for 'trash'.
independentPractice.hint: sampah; in the UK the same word can also mean 'nonsense'.

independentPractice.prompt: Your British colleague gives back the stapler she borrowed and says 'Cheers!' What does 'Cheers' mean here? One or two English words.
independentPractice.hint: No glasses, no drinks: she's just being polite.

assessment.prompt: Budi sends a voice note to a friend: 'Sorry, I gonna be late: the TransJakarta is packed.' One small word is missing for this to be correct casual English. Write the missing word.
assessment.rubric: Correct: am (I'm gonna = I am going to; I'm is the natural spoken form). 'is' / 'are' = 0 (wrong form of be after I). 'going' / 'going to' = 0 (it replaces gonna but the be is still missing). 'will' = 30 (I will be late is correct English, but it doesn't fix the gonna sentence). Anything else = 0.

assessment.prompt: Rina is applying for a scholarship at a university in Melbourne. Her email begins: 'Dear Admissions Team, I wanna know whether the application deadline can be extended.' Replace 'wanna' with formal words (two or three words) that fit: 'I ___ know whether …'
assessment.rubric: Correct: would like to (also wish to or should like to: both very formal). 'want to' = 50 (correct grammar, but plain and direct, not the polite formal choice for an application). 'would like' without 'to' = 60 (right choice, grammar slip). 'am gonna' / 'wanna to' / 'want' = 0. Anything else = 0.

assessment.prompt: Dimas at Soekarno-Hatta Airport: 'Rp 95,000 for a small iced coffee? What a rip-off!' What does 'rip-off' mean here? Answer in a few English words.
assessment.rubric: Correct: any answer meaning the price is far too high or unfair (overpriced, too expensive, not worth the money). 'expensive' alone = 70 (right direction, but a rip-off is unfairly or ridiculously expensive). 'a scam' / 'a cheat' = 80 (close: a scam is a trick to steal money; a rip-off is a price that's unfairly high). 'kemahalan' = 50 (right meaning, but the task asks for English). 'fake' / 'stolen' / 'torn' = 0 (taking 'rip' literally). Anything else = 0.

assessment.prompt: Rina is writing to a new client she has never met: 'Dear Ms Tan, Thank you for sending the brief. Your plan looks awesome, and our team can start on Monday. Kind regards, Rina' One word is slang and too informal for this email. Write it.
assessment.rubric: Correct: awesome (keren banget: fine with friends and close colleagues, but too casual for a first email to a client; better: excellent, very clear, promising). A formal replacement instead of the slang word (excellent, very good, impressive) = 70 (the right idea, but the task asks for the slang word). 'looks' / 'start' / 'kind' / 'regards' = 0. Anything else = 0.

assessment.prompt: You're having dinner with a client at a restaurant in New York. You've finished and want to pay. Complete with the American word: 'Excuse me, could we have the ___, please?'
assessment.rubric: Correct: check (American: the check = tagihan di restoran). 'bill' = 50 (the British word: Americans understand it, but the task asks for the American word). 'cheque' = 40 (British spelling of a bank cheque; the restaurant word is spelt check). 'tab' = 60 (used in American bars, less usual for a restaurant meal). 'receipt' / 'invoice' = 20 (a receipt is the proof you get after paying). Anything else = 0.

assessment.prompt: Sari checks in at a hotel in London. The receptionist says: 'Your room's on the first floor.' Later, her American colleague asks where her room is. In American English, which floor is it on? Complete: 'It's on the ___ floor.'
assessment.rubric: Correct: second (the British first floor is one level above the street, which the British call the ground floor; Americans call the street level the first floor, so one level up is the second floor). '2' = 90 (right floor, but written as a figure). 'first' = 0 (the classic trap: the same words, a different floor). 'ground' = 0. Anything else = 0.

assessment.prompt: Pak Hasan rents a car at Heathrow Airport, near London, and the tank is almost empty. He tells his colleague: 'We need to get some ___ before we drive to Oxford.' Write the British word.
assessment.rubric: Correct: petrol (bensin; American: gas, short for gasoline). 'gas' / 'gasoline' = 50 (the American word: understood, but in Britain gas usually means the gas for cooking and heating). 'fuel' = 60 (correct and neutral, but not the British word the task asks for). 'diesel' = 40 (a different fuel). 'bensin' = 20. Anything else = 0.

material.title: Gonna, wanna, gotta: informal but grammatical

id.title: Gonna, wanna, gotta: santai tapi tetap benar

blocks.text:
**Quick recap:** you already *understand* reduced forms at speed (gonna, wanna, kinda, dunno, lemme), and you know they never go in work emails. At C2 you start *using* them naturally, and that means getting their grammar right.

- **gonna** = *going to* + a verb (plans for the future). It replaces only *going to*, so the **be** (am / is / are) before it stays: **I'm gonna**, **you're gonna**, **she's gonna**, **we're gonna**, **they're gonna**. And it only goes before a verb: *I'm going **to Bandung*** (a place) never becomes 'I'm gonna Bandung'.
- **wanna** = *want to*. There's no *be* in front, but it only works where *want* has no -s: *I wanna, you wanna, they wanna*, but *she **wants to***, never 'she wanna'.
- **gotta** = *have got to* (harus). *I've gotta go*, and very often just **I gotta go**: the *'ve* disappears in speech. That's why gotta seems to break the rule above: it comes from *have got*, not from *be*.

**Why films seem to break the rule:** in quick questions, native speakers often drop the first word: *You coming?* *You gonna eat that?* (= *Are you …?*). That's normal at speed, in questions. In a statement, keep it: **I'm** gonna.

id.text:
**Ulasan singkat:** kamu sudah *memahami* bentuk-bentuk yang dipendekkan dalam ucapan cepat (gonna, wanna, kinda, dunno, lemme), dan tahu bahwa semuanya tidak pernah masuk email kerja. Di level C2 kamu mulai *memakainya* secara alami, dan itu berarti tata bahasanya harus benar.

- **gonna** = *going to* + kata kerja (rencana ke depan). Ia hanya menggantikan *going to*, jadi **be** (am / is / are) di depannya tetap ada: **I'm gonna**, **you're gonna**, **she's gonna**, **we're gonna**, **they're gonna**. Dan ia hanya dipakai sebelum kata kerja: *I'm going **to Bandung*** (tempat) tidak pernah menjadi 'I'm gonna Bandung'.
- **wanna** = *want to*. Tidak ada *be* di depannya, tapi hanya bisa dipakai kalau *want* tidak mendapat -s: *I wanna, you wanna, they wanna*, tapi *she **wants to***, tidak pernah 'she wanna'.
- **gotta** = *have got to* (harus). *I've gotta go*, dan sangat sering cukup **I gotta go**: *'ve*-nya hilang dalam ucapan. Itu sebabnya gotta seolah melanggar aturan di atas: ia berasal dari *have got*, bukan dari *be*.

**Kenapa di film aturannya seolah dilanggar:** dalam pertanyaan yang cepat, penutur asli sering membuang kata pertama: *You coming?* *You gonna eat that?* (= *Are you …?*). Itu wajar dalam ucapan cepat, dalam pertanyaan. Dalam kalimat pernyataan, pertahankan: **I'm** gonna.

rows.en: I'm gonna call you after the meeting.
rows.id: Aku telepon kamu habis rapat, ya.

rows.en: Do you wanna come with us?
Sorry, I gotta go: my ojek is here.
rows.id: Maaf, aku harus pergi: ojekku sudah datang.

blocks.text:
**The Indonesian trap.** Indonesian has no *to be*: *Aku mau telepon kamu nanti* has no word for *am*. So learners say **'I gonna call you later'**, and to a native ear it sounds like a mistake, not like relaxed English. Say **I'm gonna call you later** (speech, chats) or **I'm going to call you later** (anywhere).

**The register trap.** gonna and wanna are spoken forms. In a chat with a friend they're perfect; in an email they look careless. *Dear Sir or Madam, I wanna ask about the job* mixes the most formal opening with the most informal verb. Write **Dear Sir or Madam, I would like to ask about the job.**

id.text:
**Jebakan dari bahasa Indonesia.** Bahasa Indonesia tidak punya *to be*: *Aku mau telepon kamu nanti* tidak punya kata untuk *am*. Akibatnya pelajar bilang **'I gonna call you later'**, dan bagi telinga penutur asli itu terdengar seperti kesalahan, bukan bahasa Inggris yang santai. Ucapkan **I'm gonna call you later** (lisan, chat) atau **I'm going to call you later** (di mana saja).

**Jebakan register.** gonna dan wanna adalah bentuk lisan. Di chat dengan teman, keduanya pas; di email, terlihat asal-asalan. *Dear Sir or Madam, I wanna ask about the job* mencampur pembuka yang paling formal dengan kata kerja yang paling santai. Tulis **Dear Sir or Madam, I would like to ask about the job.**

blocks.prompt: Which sentence is correct, natural casual speech?
options: I gonna send you the photos tonight.
I'm gonna send you the photos tonight.
I'm gonna to send you the photos tonight.
blocks.explain: gonna already contains the *to* (going to → gonna), and the *be* stays: **I'm** gonna. 'I gonna' drops the *am*, the typical Indonesian slip; 'gonna to' doubles the *to*.

id.prompt: Kalimat mana yang benar dan alami untuk ucapan santai?
id.explain: gonna sudah mengandung *to* (going to → gonna), dan *be*-nya tetap ada: **I'm** gonna. 'I gonna' membuang *am*, kekeliruan khas penutur bahasa Indonesia; 'gonna to' menggandakan *to*.

material.title: Hedges, vague words and everyday informal words

id.title: Pelunak, kata-kata samar dan kosakata santai sehari-hari

blocks.text:
**Hedges and vague words** (pelunak dan kata-kata samar) make casual English sound relaxed rather than blunt or over-precise. You met them for listening; now use them:
- **kind of / sort of** = agak, semacam: *It's kind of expensive.* *I sort of agree.*
- **-ish** = sekitar, agak: *sevenish* (sekitar jam tujuh), *fortyish*, *tallish*. Alone, as an answer: 'Are you ready?' 'Ish.' (= sort of).
- **a bit** = sedikit, agak. British speakers love it for understatement: *I'm a bit annoyed* can mean quite angry.
- **or something** = atau semacamnya; **and stuff / and things** = dan lain-lain.
Use them in conversation and chats. In a report or a formal email, be precise (*at approximately 7 p.m.*) or use the formal hedges from C1 (*appears to*, *it is likely that*).

**Everyday informal words** you can actually use with friends and relaxed colleagues:
- **reckon** = think, guess (kayaknya). Very common in British and Australian English; to many Americans it sounds rural or old-fashioned.
- **fancy** (British) = want, feel like: *Fancy a coffee?* (Mau ngopi?), *I fancy noodles tonight.*
- **cheers** (British) = thanks, or bye, and also the word for a toast (bersulang).
- **mate** (UK, Australia) = friend; also a friendly way to address someone, mostly between men.
- **guys**: *Hi guys! / you guys* = everyone, women included, in casual US and UK English. In written messages at work, *Hi all* or *Hi everyone* is the safer choice.
- **no worries** = no problem / you're welcome (Australian, now common everywhere).
- **my bad** = my mistake (American, casual; only for small mistakes).
- **to be fair** (British) = adds a point on the other side, to be fair to someone (tapi harus diakui).
- **you know what I mean?** = checks the listener is with you (ngerti kan maksudku?). Useful, but after every sentence it gets tiring.

id.text:
**Pelunak dan kata-kata samar** membuat bahasa Inggris santai terdengar rileks, tidak terlalu blak-blakan atau terlalu persis. Kamu sudah mengenalnya untuk menyimak; sekarang pakailah:
- **kind of / sort of** = agak, semacam: *It's kind of expensive.* *I sort of agree.*
- **-ish** = sekitar, agak: *sevenish* (sekitar jam tujuh), *fortyish* (sekitar empat puluhan), *tallish* (agak tinggi). Sendirian, sebagai jawaban: 'Are you ready?' 'Ish.' (= ya, kurang lebih).
- **a bit** = sedikit, agak. Orang Inggris suka memakainya untuk mengecilkan sesuatu: *I'm a bit annoyed* bisa berarti cukup marah.
- **or something** = atau semacamnya; **and stuff / and things** = dan lain-lain.
Pakai di obrolan dan chat. Di laporan atau email formal, tulislah dengan persis (*at approximately 7 p.m.*) atau pakai pelunak formal dari C1 (*appears to*, *it is likely that*).

**Kosakata santai sehari-hari** yang benar-benar bisa kamu pakai dengan teman dan rekan kerja yang santai:
- **reckon** = rasa, kira (kayaknya). Sangat umum di bahasa Inggris Inggris dan Australia; bagi banyak orang Amerika terdengar seperti orang desa atau kuno.
- **fancy** (Inggris) = mau, sedang ingin: *Fancy a coffee?* (Mau ngopi?), *I fancy noodles tonight.* (Malam ini aku pengin mi.)
- **cheers** (Inggris) = makasih, atau dah, dan juga kata untuk bersulang.
- **mate** (Inggris, Australia) = teman; juga sapaan akrab untuk orang lain, kebanyakan antar laki-laki.
- **guys**: *Hi guys! / you guys* = semuanya, termasuk perempuan, dalam bahasa Inggris santai di AS dan Inggris. Di pesan tertulis di kantor, *Hi all* atau *Hi everyone* lebih aman.
- **no worries** = nggak masalah / sama-sama (dari Australia, sekarang umum di mana-mana).
- **my bad** = salahku (Amerika, santai; hanya untuk kesalahan kecil).
- **to be fair** (Inggris) = menambahkan poin dari sisi lain, supaya adil pada seseorang (tapi harus diakui).
- **you know what I mean?** = memastikan pendengar mengikuti (ngerti kan maksudku?). Berguna, tapi kalau diucapkan setiap kalimat jadi melelahkan.

rows.en: I reckon we'll finish by Friday.
rows.id: Kayaknya kita bakal selesai hari Jumat.

rows.en: Fancy a coffee after the meeting?
Sorry, my bad: I sent you the old file.
rows.id: Maaf, salahku: aku kirim file yang lama.

rows.en: The food took ages. To be fair, it was the first evening of Ramadan.
rows.id: Makanannya lama sekali. Tapi harus diakui, itu malam pertama Ramadan.

rows.en: We could get bakso or something.
rows.id: Kita bisa makan bakso atau apa gitu.

blocks.text: **Watch the false friend *fancy*.** Indonesians know *fancy* as an adjective: *a fancy restaurant* = restoran mewah. In British English it's also a verb meaning *want*: *Fancy a walk?* has nothing to do with luxury. And with a person it means attraction: *Rina fancies Dimas* = Rina naksir Dimas. So *Fancy a drink?* is a friendly invitation, but *I fancy you* is a romantic confession.

id.text: **Hati-hati dengan teman palsu *fancy*.** Orang Indonesia mengenal *fancy* sebagai kata sifat: *a fancy restaurant* = restoran mewah. Dalam bahasa Inggris Inggris, *fancy* juga kata kerja yang berarti *mau*: *Fancy a walk?* tidak ada hubungannya dengan kemewahan. Dan kalau objeknya orang, artinya tertarik: *Rina fancies Dimas* = Rina naksir Dimas. Jadi *Fancy a drink?* adalah ajakan ramah, tapi *I fancy you* adalah pengakuan cinta.

blocks.prompt: A British colleague says: 'The new manager is strict. To be fair, she did warn us about the deadline back in January.' What does 'To be fair' do here?
options: It adds a point in the manager's favour, to balance the criticism.
It says the manager treats everyone equally.
It says the speaker thinks the deadline was unfair.
blocks.explain: **to be fair** introduces a point on the other side: the manager is strict, but she did warn them, so the criticism is softened (tapi harus diakui). It isn't a comment on the manager being fair or the deadline being unfair.

id.prompt: Seorang rekan kerja dari Inggris berkata: 'The new manager is strict. To be fair, she did warn us about the deadline back in January.' Apa fungsi 'To be fair' di sini?
id.explain: **to be fair** membuka poin dari sisi lain: manajernya memang tegas, tapi dia sudah memperingatkan mereka, jadi kritiknya diperlunak (tapi harus diakui). Ini bukan komentar bahwa manajernya adil atau tenggatnya tidak adil.
options: Menambahkan hal yang mendukung manajer untuk menyeimbangkan kritik.
Menyatakan manajer memperlakukan semua orang dengan adil.
Menyatakan pembicara menganggap tenggatnya tidak adil.

material.title: Slang: understand lots, use a little

blocks.text:
**Slang** = very informal words, often new, often used by one group (young people, gamers, one city or country). You already know how it works from **bahasa gaul**: *mager* (malas gerak), *gabut* or *anjay* are fine with friends, but nobody says *Maaf, Pak, saya mager* to a director. Some gaul words sound old after a few years, and some are rude to some people. English slang works exactly the same way.

**1. Common, fairly safe slang** (casual talk with friends and relaxed colleagues; not in formal writing):
- **cool** = good, fine (*That's cool* = it's fine, nggak apa-apa) · **awesome** = great (keren banget; American, now global) · **chill** = relaxed (santai), *chill out* = relax
- **broke** = with no money (bokek) · **a rip-off** = far too expensive, unfair (kemahalan); as a verb: *they ripped us off*
- **a buck** = one US dollar (*ten bucks*) · **a quid** = one British pound (*ten quid*, never 'ten quids')
- **FOMO** = fear of missing out (takut ketinggalan), now even used in advertising

**2. Younger and internet slang** (understand it; use it only with people who use it):
- **sus** = suspicious (mencurigakan) · **lowkey** = a little, secretly (*I lowkey want to quit*) · **highkey** = openly, very
- **vibe** = atmosphere, feeling (*a nice vibe*) · **ghost someone** = suddenly stop replying, with no explanation (menghilang tanpa kabar)

**3. Slang dates fast and belongs to groups.** *groovy* sounds like the 1970s, and words that were everywhere online a few years ago can sound embarrassing now. *sick* means great to many young speakers but ill to everyone else. From a 45-year-old manager, *lowkey* can sound like trying too hard.

**4. Offensive slang** exists, and this course doesn't teach it. Swear words and insults about groups of people can end a meeting, or a job. You'll hear some in films and series; that doesn't make them safe to repeat.

id.text:
**Slang** = kata-kata yang sangat santai, sering baru, sering dipakai oleh satu kelompok (anak muda, gamer, satu kota atau negara). Kamu sudah tahu cara kerjanya dari **bahasa gaul**: *mager* (malas gerak), *gabut* atau *anjay* tidak masalah dengan teman, tapi tidak ada yang bilang *Maaf, Pak, saya mager* ke direktur. Sebagian kata gaul terdengar kuno setelah beberapa tahun, dan sebagian dianggap kasar oleh sebagian orang. Slang bahasa Inggris bekerja persis sama.

**1. Slang yang umum dan cukup aman** (obrolan santai dengan teman dan rekan kerja yang santai; bukan di tulisan formal):
- **cool** = bagus, oke (*That's cool* = nggak apa-apa) · **awesome** = keren banget (Amerika, sekarang mendunia) · **chill** = santai, *chill out* = bersantai
- **broke** = tidak punya uang (bokek) · **a rip-off** = jauh terlalu mahal, tidak masuk akal (kemahalan); sebagai kata kerja: *they ripped us off* (kita dikerjai soal harga)
- **a buck** = satu dolar AS (*ten bucks*) · **a quid** = satu pound Inggris (*ten quid*, tidak pernah 'ten quids')
- **FOMO** = fear of missing out (takut ketinggalan), sekarang bahkan dipakai di iklan

**2. Slang anak muda dan internet** (pahami; pakai hanya dengan orang yang memakainya):
- **sus** = mencurigakan (dari *suspicious*) · **lowkey** = agak, diam-diam (*I lowkey want to quit*) · **highkey** = terang-terangan, banget
- **vibe** = suasana, rasa (*a nice vibe*) · **ghost someone** = tiba-tiba berhenti membalas, tanpa penjelasan (menghilang tanpa kabar)

**3. Slang cepat basi dan milik kelompok tertentu.** *groovy* terdengar seperti tahun 1970-an, dan kata-kata yang beberapa tahun lalu ada di mana-mana di internet sekarang bisa terdengar memalukan. *sick* berarti keren bagi banyak anak muda, tapi sakit bagi semua orang lainnya. Dari mulut manajer berusia 45 tahun, *lowkey* bisa terdengar terlalu memaksa.

**4. Slang yang kasar** itu ada, dan kursus ini tidak mengajarkannya. Kata makian dan hinaan terhadap kelompok orang bisa merusak rapat, atau karier. Kamu akan mendengar sebagian di film dan serial; itu tidak membuatnya aman untuk ditiru.

rows.en: Work email: The quotation seems rather high. Could you review it?
rows.id: Email kerja: Penawaran harganya tampak cukup tinggi. Bisakah Anda meninjaunya kembali?

blocks.text: **At work: three questions.** Before you use slang, ask: **Who** is it for (a friend, your team, a director, a client you've never met)? **Where** (a chat, a meeting, an email, a report)? **Would they use this word themselves?** If all three point to casual and yes, a little slang is fine. If not, choose a neutral word: *broke* → *short of money*, *a rip-off* → *overpriced*, *awesome* → *excellent*. And the golden rule: **when in doubt, leave it out.**

id.text: **Di tempat kerja: tiga pertanyaan.** Sebelum memakai slang, tanyakan: **Untuk siapa** (teman, timmu, direktur, klien yang belum pernah kamu temui)? **Di mana** (chat, rapat, email, laporan)? **Apakah mereka sendiri akan memakai kata ini?** Kalau ketiganya mengarah ke santai dan ya, sedikit slang tidak masalah. Kalau tidak, pilih kata netral: *broke* → *short of money*, *a rip-off* → *overpriced*, *awesome* → *excellent*. Dan aturan emasnya: **kalau ragu, jangan dipakai** (*when in doubt, leave it out*).

blocks.prompt: Bu Ani, the finance director, is writing to a supplier whose prices have gone up 40%. Which sentence fits her email?
options: Your new prices are a total rip-off.
Your new prices are kind of sus, to be honest.
We are concerned that your new prices are significantly higher than the market rate.
blocks.explain: A director's email to a supplier needs neutral or formal words: **significantly higher than the market rate** says the same thing without insulting anyone. *a rip-off* and *sus* are slang: in a work email they sound rude and unprofessional.

id.prompt: Bu Ani, direktur keuangan, menulis kepada pemasok yang harganya naik 40%. Kalimat mana yang cocok untuk emailnya?
id.explain: Email direktur kepada pemasok butuh kata-kata netral atau formal: **significantly higher than the market rate** menyampaikan hal yang sama tanpa menyinggung siapa pun. *a rip-off* dan *sus* adalah slang: di email kerja keduanya terdengar kasar dan tidak profesional.

blocks.text:
British (UK) and American (US) English share almost all their words, and everyone understands both. A few everyday words differ, though, and a few can confuse or embarrass you. You met *lift / elevator*, *flat / apartment* and *holiday / vacation* at C1; here is the full everyday set.

**Bridge from Indonesian:** we already say **lift** and **CV**, like the British (Americans say *elevator* and *résumé*). We also say *HP* or *handphone*, which neither country uses: say **mobile** (UK) or **cell phone** (US).

**What to do:** understand both, and choose one variety for your own writing (spelling too: *colour / color*). Either one is correct; consistency is what looks professional.

id.text:
Bahasa Inggris Inggris (UK) dan Amerika (US) memakai hampir semua kata yang sama, dan semua orang memahami keduanya. Tapi beberapa kata sehari-hari berbeda, dan beberapa bisa membingungkan atau membuatmu malu. Kamu sudah bertemu *lift / elevator*, *flat / apartment* dan *holiday / vacation* di C1; ini daftar lengkap untuk sehari-hari.

**Jembatan dari bahasa Indonesia:** kita sudah bilang **lift** dan **CV**, seperti orang Inggris (orang Amerika bilang *elevator* dan *résumé*). Kita juga bilang *HP* atau *handphone*, yang tidak dipakai di kedua negara itu: bilang **mobile** (UK) atau **cell phone** (US).

**Yang perlu dilakukan:** pahami keduanya, dan pilih satu ragam untuk tulisanmu sendiri (ejaannya juga: *colour / color*). Keduanya benar; yang terlihat profesional adalah konsistensi.

blocks.text:
**The two traps that cause real embarrassment or confusion.**
- **pants**: in the US, *pants* = trousers. In the UK, *pants* = underwear (celana dalam). 'I like your pants' to a British colleague gets a laugh, or a very awkward silence. In the UK, say **trousers**.
- **floors**: the US, like most Indonesian houses and offices, calls the street level floor 1 (*lantai 1*). The UK calls it the **ground floor**, so the British **first floor** is one level up: the American *second floor* (usually your *lantai 2*; a mall with a *Lantai Dasar* counts like the UK). When a London receptionist says 'first floor', go up one level.

id.text:
**Dua jebakan yang benar-benar bisa memalukan atau membingungkan.**
- **pants**: di AS, *pants* = celana panjang. Di Inggris, *pants* = celana dalam. 'I like your pants' kepada rekan kerja dari Inggris akan membuatnya tertawa, atau membuat suasana sangat canggung. Di Inggris, bilang **trousers**.
- **lantai**: AS, seperti kebanyakan rumah dan kantor di Indonesia, menyebut lantai di level jalan sebagai lantai 1 (*first floor*). Inggris menyebutnya **ground floor**, jadi **first floor** versi Inggris adalah satu lantai di atasnya: *second floor* versi Amerika (biasanya *lantai 2* kita; mal yang punya *Lantai Dasar* menghitung seperti Inggris). Kalau resepsionis di London bilang 'first floor', naiklah satu lantai.

blocks.prompt: Your American client in Chicago says: 'Let's meet on the sidewalk outside my office, by the coffee cart.' Where will you wait?
options: On the road, next to the cars.
On the footpath beside the road (trotoar).
blocks.explain: **sidewalk** (US) = **pavement** (UK) = trotoar. Careful: in American English *pavement* means the road surface, so the British word can confuse an American.

id.prompt: Klien Amerikamu di Chicago berkata: 'Let's meet on the sidewalk outside my office, by the coffee cart.' Di mana kamu akan menunggu?
id.explain: **sidewalk** (AS) = **pavement** (Inggris) = trotoar. Hati-hati: dalam bahasa Inggris Amerika *pavement* berarti permukaan jalan, jadi kata versi Inggris bisa membingungkan orang Amerika.
options: Di badan jalan, di samping mobil.

resources.title: Go from 'Basic' to 'Fire'! Learn Gen Z Phrases and Slang
resources.source: Learning English with Oxford (Oxford University Press)
resources.note: Fifteen pieces of Gen Z slang from 2020 with their meanings (basic, extra, FOMO, glow-up, salty, spill the tea, vibe …). Read it as a lesson in how fast slang dates: some of these already sound old. A few (snack, slide into someone's DMs) are about dating and flirting: understand them, but keep them out of work. The blog is archived, so the comments may not load.

id.note: Lima belas slang Gen Z dari tahun 2020 beserta artinya (basic, extra, FOMO, glow-up, salty, spill the tea, vibe …). Bacalah sebagai bukti betapa cepatnya slang basi: sebagian sudah terdengar kuno. Beberapa (snack, slide into someone's DMs) tentang kencan dan menggoda: pahami, tapi jangan dipakai di kantor. Blognya sudah diarsipkan, jadi kolom komentarnya mungkin tidak muncul.

id.intro: Kamu sudah memahami bahasa Inggris santai dalam kecepatan penuh: gonna, dunno, kinda, dan slang film seperti I'm down dan gutted. Sekarang saatnya memakainya sendiri, dengan penilaian yang tepat: kata-kata santai yang membuatmu terdengar rileks (reckon, fancy, no worries), slang yang aman dan yang tidak, serta kata-kata Inggris dan Amerika yang berbeda (di London, jangan pernah memuji 'pants' seseorang!). Pemanasan: kata bahasa gaul apa yang kamu pakai dengan teman tapi tidak pernah di rapat?
suggestedQuestions: Bolehkah saya bilang 'Hi guys' di rapat tim?
Sebaiknya saya belajar bahasa Inggris versi Inggris atau Amerika?
Bagaimana mengatakan 'mager' atau 'gabut' dalam bahasa Inggris?

assessment.cls-1: Budi mengirim pesan suara ke temannya: 'Sorry, I gonna be late: the TransJakarta is packed.' Ada satu kata kecil yang hilang supaya ini menjadi bahasa Inggris santai yang benar. Tulis kata yang hilang itu.
assessment.cls-2: Rina mendaftar beasiswa di sebuah universitas di Melbourne. Emailnya dimulai seperti ini: 'Dear Admissions Team, I wanna know whether the application deadline can be extended.' Ganti 'wanna' dengan kata-kata formal dalam bahasa Inggris (dua atau tiga kata) yang cocok: 'I ___ know whether …'
assessment.cls-3: Dimas di Bandara Soekarno-Hatta: 'Rp 95,000 for a small iced coffee? What a rip-off!' Apa arti 'rip-off' di sini? Jawab dengan beberapa kata dalam bahasa Inggris.
assessment.cls-4: Rina menulis kepada klien baru yang belum pernah ia temui: 'Dear Ms Tan, Thank you for sending the brief. Your plan looks awesome, and our team can start on Monday. Kind regards, Rina' Ada satu kata slang yang terlalu santai untuk email ini. Tulis kata itu.
assessment.cls-5: Kamu makan malam dengan klien di sebuah restoran di New York. Kalian sudah selesai dan ingin membayar. Lengkapi dengan kata versi Amerika: 'Excuse me, could we have the ___, please?'
assessment.cls-6: Sari check-in di sebuah hotel di London. Resepsionis berkata: 'Your room's on the first floor.' Kemudian rekan kerjanya dari Amerika bertanya di mana kamarnya. Dalam bahasa Inggris Amerika, kamarnya di lantai berapa? Lengkapi: 'It's on the ___ floor.'
assessment.cls-7: Pak Hasan menyewa mobil di Bandara Heathrow, dekat London, dan tangkinya hampir kosong. Ia berkata kepada rekannya: 'We need to get some ___ before we drive to Oxford.' Tulis kata versi Inggris (UK).
